title: Tenant Segregation Matrix and Routing Guidance for Hosted/Dedicated/Private
summary: Working notes that compare tenant segregation patterns across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Includes a lightweight matrix for choosing isolation boundaries, recommended routing primitives, operational considerations for multi-region control plane, and open questions for security and cost trade-offs.
content:
Purpose:
This is a pragmatic, implementation-focused note aimed at Platform, Serving Runtime, and SRE teams. We want a concise decision matrix for how tenant traffic is routed and where isolation boundaries live across the three commercial deployment modes: Hosted (multi-tenant cloud), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools / customer tenancy on shared infra), and Private (VPC / on-prem customer-controlled).

Context and motivation:
- Past incidents: two production regressions where mis-routed KV cache keys caused cross-tenant latency spikes (postmortem references in JIRA-PLAT-1127).
- Product requirements: predictable latency SLOs for Dedicated, strong network/data isolation for Private, and cost-multiplexing for Hosted.
- Goal: provide a single set of recommended routing primitives that can be parameterized per deployment mode to reduce ad-hoc implementations in the wild.

High-level guidance (one-line):
- Hosted: favor logical isolation (namespaces + auth-based routing) with aggressive shared caching and fallback model variants; enforce strict tenant-aware request headers and runtime request tagging.
- Dedicated: favor physical isolation at the serving pool level (customer-id -> pool mapping), keep shared control plane but isolate data plane routing and KV caches per-tenant/pool.
- Private: push control-plane out of customer network as much as possible, but default to tenant-controlled data-plane endpoints (private ingress) with zero shared mutable state.

Segregation matrix (decision factors):
(we present this as a short list — use this to choose the routing pattern)
- Security sensitivity: High => Private; Medium => Dedicated; Low => Hosted.
- Performance determinism: High => Dedicated (reserved pools); Medium => Private (customer HW variability); Low => Hosted (best-effort shared).
- Cost sensitivity: High => Hosted; Medium => Dedicated; Low => Private (customer bears infra).
- Operational ownership preference: Customer-op => Private; Redwood-managed => Hosted/Dedicated.

Routing primitives we recommend (composition of simple building blocks):
1) Global control-plane router (CP-router): central service for registration, pool metadata, region mapping, and policy enforcement. Lightweight — no per-request payload transformation.
2) Per-region front door (edge-router): layer that terminates client TLS, performs tenant auth lookup, enriches requests with tenant-id, and does early routing decisions (region vs fallback).
3) Pool-level data-plane routers (pool-proxies): serve as the last-mile router inside a region/pool. They resolve model variant, cache shard, quantization profile, and direct to an inference worker.
4) Tenant-scoped caches: KV and prefix caches that are optionally namespaced per-tenant.
5) Fallback lanes: pre-defined compatible models/pools used during capacity shortages.

Patterns by deployment mode (concrete):
- Hosted pattern (preferred primitives):
  * Control-plane: global CP-router fully managed on Redwood multi-region control plane.
  * Edge-router: public global front doors in each region. Tenant auth is via API key + signed request header.
  * Data-plane: multi-tenant pools, pooling across tenants. Caches are by default shared but with tenant-aware keys (prefixing).
  * Isolation boundary: logical (tenant-id prefixing + runtime tag checks).
  * Routing policy: latency-first for free-tier; cost-aware for burst/low-priority traffic (route to cheaper quantized models).
  * Failover: automated region failover + model-fallback policy anchored in CP-router.

- Dedicated pattern (preferred primitives):
  * Control-plane: Redwood-managed CP-router but with tenant-specific pool allocations and capacity hints.
  * Edge-router: same public front doors, but request mapping consults tenant->pool mapping before selecting shared pools.
  * Data-plane: dedicated pools (reserved GPU nodes) for each customer when committed; pool-proxies enforce tenant affinity.
  * Isolation boundary: physical (pool boundary) + runtime checks. Caches default to per-tenant instances to avoid noisy neighbor caching.
  * Routing policy: throughput-first within pool, strict rate-limits per-tenant; optional burst lanes that can spill to hosted pools under configured SLAs.
  * Failover: configured canary and fallback to designated spillover pools (usually other Dedicated pools or safe-hosted fallbacks).

- Private pattern (preferred primitives):
  * Control-plane: minimal central CP-router (control plane can be hosted but optionally deployed in customer VPC). CP-router should not have access to customer keys or sensitive config in plain text.
  * Edge-router: customer-controlled ingress (private load balancer / direct peering). Redwood agents run inside customer network for service discovery.
  * Data-plane: customer-owned nodes, single-tenant by default, no shared caches. Where shared infra exists internally, enforce flat mappings to tenant id = customer.
  * Isolation boundary: network + tenant ownership. No shared runtime mutable state across customers.
  * Routing policy: handle local policies (routing by subnets, IAM roles). CP-router is a policy-orchestration only.
  * Failover: customer-defined; Redwood does not automatically move workloads out of customer environment without explicit config.

Detailed operational notes:
- Tenant identity propagation: everywhere the request traverses, a tenant-id header (x-rw-tenant-id) + signature must be present. Edge-router validates auth and signs a short-lived internal token for pool-proxies.
- Cache key hygiene: always include tenant-id in prefix for caches unless explicitly opting into cross-tenant sharing. For Hosted, create a "shared-cache opt-in mechanism" for select low-sensitivity workloads.
- KV cache eviction and memory accounting: Dedicated pools expose per-tenant memory quotas. CP-router stores per-pool capacity metadata to help edge-router choose low-memory-pressure pools.
- Circuit breakers: pool-proxies implement per-tenant circuit breakers (latency/error threshold) and bubble up health metrics to CP-router. CP-router triggers routing changes when health degrades.
- Telemetry: every hop emits trace/metric containing tenant-id, pool-id, model-variant, quantization flags. Tagging is critical for cost allocation and debug.
- Compliance: Private deployment must support KMS/HSM key ownership by customer. Do not persist unencrypted tenant-sensitive metadata in shared control plane logs.

Multi-region control-plane considerations:
- Control plane goals: make it authoritative for topology and policy but small/immutable for per-request decisions.
- Data replication: metadata (pool registry, tenant->pool mappings) is replicated on a best-effort + read-optimized schedule. For strong decisions (e.g., immediate capacity changes), prefer lease-based ephemeral tokens rather than synchronous writes.
- Regional failover: when regional edge loses connectivity, edge-router should consult local stale read of mapping and apply conservative fallbacks (e.g., route to cross-region compatible pool).
- Split-brain: CP-router should elect a single-write leader with read replicas; use leases with TTLs to avoid conflicting pool assignments.

Security and data-leakage risks (and mitigations):
- Risk: shared caches exposing tokenized or semi-structured output across tenants. Mitigation: default tenant-keyed caches + automated audits to detect cross-tenant cache hits.
- Risk: control-plane configuration leak exposing tenant IP ranges or dedicated pool topology. Mitigation: obfuscate sensitive metadata in global logs; provide scoped views in UI/console and mask sensitive fields in telemetry.
- Risk: credential replay at edge-router. Mitigation: ephemeral internal tokens, signature-based headers, and short TTLs for internal tokens.

Cost & capacity trade-offs (practical knobs):
- Hosted: tune cache sharing ratio and batch size per model family to reduce per-token cost.
- Dedicated: reserve memory and GPU partitioning that favors workload determinism; implement CPU/GPU overcommit throttles only with explicit tenant consent.
- Private: expect operational variability; provide sizing calculators for common model families and allow Redwood to suggest quantization profiles to lower footprint.

Operational playbook snippets (runbook style):
- Adding a tenant to Dedicated: 1) allocate pool in CP-router 2) assign pool-id and capacity metadata 3) provision pool-proxies with tenant config 4) warm caches, run synthetic tests, 5) flip route in edge-router.
- Incident: cross-tenant latency spike: 1) identify impacted pool-id via telemetry 2) isolate pool-proxy and check per-tenant circuit breakers 3) if shared-cache hot-key suspected, invalidate keys and throttle offending tenant 4) if unresolved, failover to backup pool and escalate.

Compatibility and migration notes:
- Dedicated <-> Hosted fallbacks: only allowed when customer opts-in. We must document SLA changes in control-plane and billing.
- Private to Hosted migration: create explicit export of model artifacts + customer keys (if permitted) and require customer approval before moving data out.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Should Hosted offer a fully tenant-dedicated cache tier as a paid add-on? (Pros: less noisy neighbors. Cons: operational complexity in autoscaling.)
- How strict must CP-router be about model-variant compatibility when performing cross-pool failover? (We currently describe compatibility as a conservative subset; need test harnesses.)
- For Private deployments, what telemetry subset is permissible to send to hosted control plane for global metrics without violating customer expectations?

Next steps / action items:
- Platform-engineering: prototype a tenant-keyed cache middleware and run a 2-week A/B test on a low-sensitivity Hosted model family. Owner: Noah Chen. (JIRA-PLAT-1127)
- SRE: create detection rule for cross-tenant cache hits and alert on >0.1% cross-hit rate. Owner: Priya Singh.
- Product: define billing language and opt-in flow for Dedicated->Hosted spillover. Owner: María Ortega.

Notes to reviewers: this doc is intentionally prescriptive but lightweight — aim is to converge on an explicit set of primitives rather than micro-architecture. Please comment on the matrix decisions and the open questions.
